notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Cropping pattern refers to the proportion of cultivated land devoted to different crops in a particular region and period.
  • It reflects the combination and sequence of crops grown by farmers.
  • Cropping pattern varies according to climate, soil, irrigation, prices and food demand.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cropping Pattern → What Crops + How Much Area + In What Sequence

2. Factors Determining Cropping Pattern

Major factors include:

  • Rainfall.
  • Temperature.
  • Soil.
  • Irrigation.
  • Relief.
  • Market demand.
  • Crop prices.
  • Technology.
  • Labour.
  • Government support.
3. Physical Factors

Important physical factors are:

  • Climate.
  • Soil fertility.
  • Topography.
  • Water availability.
  • Length of growing season.
4. Economic Factors

Economic influences include:

  • Market price.
  • Input cost.
  • Transport.
  • Storage.
  • Processing facilities.
  • Export demand.
5. Technological Factors

Cropping patterns are altered by:

  • Irrigation.
  • Improved seeds.
  • Mechanisation.
  • Fertilisers.
  • Micro-irrigation.
  • Cold storage.
6. Crop Season and Cropping Pattern

India's cropping pattern is organised mainly around:

  • Kharif.
  • Rabi.
  • Zaid.
7. Kharif Crops

Kharif crops are generally:

  • Sown during June-July.
  • Grown during southwest monsoon.
  • Harvested from September onward.

Important examples:

  • Rice.
  • Maize.
  • Cotton.
  • Groundnut.
  • Soybean.
  • Bajra.
  • Tur.
8. Rabi Crops

Rabi crops are generally:

  • Sown in winter.
  • Harvested in spring.

Important examples:

  • Wheat.
  • Barley.
  • Gram.
  • Mustard.
  • Peas.
9. Zaid Crops

Zaid crops are grown in the short summer period between Rabi and Kharif.

Examples include:

  • Watermelon.
  • Muskmelon.
  • Cucumber.
  • Vegetables.
  • Fodder.
10. Food-Grain Crops

Food grains include:

  • Cereals.
  • Millets.
  • Pulses.

Major cereals include:

  • Rice.
  • Wheat.
  • Maize.
11. Rice — Basic Importance
  • Rice is one of India's most important food crops.
  • It is the staple food of large parts of eastern, southern and northeastern India.
  • It is primarily a Kharif crop, although irrigation allows multiple rice seasons in some regions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rice → Mainly Kharif Crop

12. Rice Climatic Requirements

Rice generally requires:

  • Warm temperature.
  • High humidity.
  • Abundant water during growth.
  • Frost-free conditions.
13. Rice Temperature
  • Rice grows best under warm conditions.
  • Temperatures around the mid-20s°C are generally favourable during much of the growing season.
14. Rice Rainfall
  • Rice is well suited to areas receiving high rainfall.
  • In lower-rainfall regions, irrigation is essential.
15. Rice and Standing Water
  • Paddy fields are commonly flooded or kept saturated during important growth stages.
  • Standing water helps suppress weeds and maintain soil moisture.
16. Rice Soil

Rice grows well in:

  • Clayey soils.
  • Alluvial soils.
  • Deltaic soils.
  • Soils capable of retaining water.
17. Major Rice Regions

Important rice-growing regions include:

  • West Bengal.
  • Uttar Pradesh.
  • Bihar.
  • Odisha.
  • Chhattisgarh.
  • Assam.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Telangana.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Punjab.
  • Haryana.
18. Eastern India and Rice
  • Eastern India has extensive rice cultivation because of:
  • High monsoon rainfall.
  • Fertile alluvial soils.
  • Large river plains.
19. Rice in Punjab and Haryana
  • Rice is cultivated extensively with irrigation.
  • It is not the traditional crop best suited to the semi-arid natural climate.
  • Heavy irrigation has contributed to groundwater stress.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Punjab Rice → Mainly Irrigation-Supported

20. Rice in Coastal Plains

Rice is important in:

  • Mahanadi delta.
  • Godavari delta.
  • Krishna delta.
  • Kaveri delta.
📌 Must-Memorise

Major East-Coast Deltas → Rice

21. Rice Cultivation Methods

Common methods include:

  • Broadcasting.
  • Direct seeding.
  • Transplantation.
22. Transplantation
  • Rice seedlings are first raised in nurseries.
  • They are later transplanted into prepared fields.
  • This allows better plant spacing and weed management.
23. Direct-Seeded Rice
  • Seeds are directly sown in the main field.
  • This can reduce labour and water use compared with conventional puddled transplantation under suitable conditions.
24. System of Rice Intensification
  • SRI is a rice-management approach involving:
  • Younger seedlings.
  • Wider spacing.
  • Controlled water.
  • Improved soil aeration.
  • It aims to improve water and input efficiency.
25. Rice Seasons in Tamil Nadu

Important rice seasons include:

  • Kuruvai.
  • Samba.
  • Thaladi.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

TN Paddy → Kuruvai + Samba + Thaladi

26. Kuruvai
  • Kuruvai is a short-duration rice crop.
  • It is especially important in the Kaveri delta.
  • It depends heavily on timely irrigation.
27. Samba
  • Samba is a longer-duration paddy crop.
  • It is closely linked with northeast monsoon rainfall and irrigation.
28. Thaladi
  • Thaladi is another important rice season in the Kaveri delta.
  • It follows earlier crop cycles depending on water availability.
29. Kaveri Delta Rice
  • Kaveri delta is Tamil Nadu's most famous paddy-growing region.
  • Fertile alluvial soil and canal irrigation favour rice cultivation.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Kaveri Delta → Rice Bowl of Tamil Nadu

30. Wheat — Basic Importance
  • Wheat is India's major Rabi cereal.
  • It is the principal food grain of northwestern and northern India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Wheat → Rabi Crop

31. Wheat Climate

Wheat generally requires:

  • Cool growing season.
  • Moderate moisture.
  • Dry and warm weather during ripening.
32. Wheat Rainfall
  • Moderate rainfall is favourable.
  • Excessive rainfall during ripening can damage the crop.
  • Irrigation is important in drier northwestern regions.
33. Wheat Soil

Wheat grows well in:

  • Fertile alluvial soils.
  • Well-drained loamy soils.
  • Some black-soil regions.
34. Major Wheat Regions

Important wheat-growing regions include:

  • Uttar Pradesh.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Punjab.
  • Haryana.
  • Rajasthan.
  • Bihar.
35. Wheat and Northwestern India

Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh have favourable:

  • Irrigation.
  • Level land.
  • Mechanisation.
  • Fertile soils.
  • Green Revolution infrastructure.
36. Wheat and Green Revolution
  • Wheat was the major early beneficiary of India's Green Revolution.
  • High-yielding varieties greatly increased production in irrigated northwestern India.
37. Western Disturbances and Wheat
  • Light winter rainfall from western disturbances benefits wheat in northwestern India.
  • Excessive rain or hail can damage standing crops.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Western Disturbance → Useful for Rabi Wheat

38. Rice vs Wheat

Rice:

  • Warm and wet.
  • Mainly Kharif.
  • Greater water requirement.

Wheat:

  • Cool growing season.
  • Rabi.
  • Moderate water requirement.
39. Maize — Basic Facts
  • Maize is an important cereal and feed crop.
  • It is mainly grown as a Kharif crop, though it can be cultivated in other seasons under suitable conditions.
40. Uses of Maize

Maize is used for:

  • Human food.
  • Poultry feed.
  • Livestock feed.
  • Starch.
  • Industrial processing.
41. Maize Climate

Maize prefers:

  • Warm conditions.
  • Moderate rainfall.
  • Well-drained soil.

Waterlogging is harmful.

42. Maize Soil
  • Fertile, well-drained loamy soils are favourable.
43. Major Maize Regions

Important maize-growing states include:

  • Karnataka.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Bihar.
  • Telangana.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Rajasthan.
44. Millets

Important millets include:

  • Jowar.
  • Bajra.
  • Ragi.
  • Small millets.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Millets → Dryland Crops

45. Importance of Millets

Millets generally:

  • Require less water than paddy.
  • Tolerate dry conditions.
  • Grow in relatively poor soils.
  • Are nutritionally rich.
46. Jowar
  • Jowar is sorghum.
  • It is an important cereal of semi-arid India.
  • It can be grown in both Kharif and Rabi seasons depending on region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jowar = Sorghum

47. Jowar Climate

Jowar is suited to:

  • Warm climate.
  • Moderate to low rainfall.
  • Semi-arid conditions.
48. Jowar Soils
  • Black soils are particularly suitable in parts of the Deccan.
  • Well-drained soils are preferred.
49. Jowar Regions

Important regions include:

  • Maharashtra.
  • Karnataka.
  • Telangana.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
50. Bajra
  • Bajra is pearl millet.
  • It is highly drought tolerant.
  • It is well suited to hot, dry regions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Bajra = Pearl Millet

51. Bajra Regions

Important regions include:

  • Rajasthan.
  • Gujarat.
  • Haryana.
  • Uttar Pradesh.
  • Maharashtra.
52. Bajra Soil
  • Bajra can grow on sandy and relatively poor soils.
  • It is well adapted to arid and semi-arid environments.
53. Rajasthan and Bajra
  • Bajra is one of Rajasthan's most characteristic food crops.
  • It tolerates low and variable rainfall.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rajasthan → Bajra

54. Ragi
  • Ragi is finger millet.
  • It is important in southern India.
  • It is a nutritious cereal rich in calcium.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ragi = Finger Millet

55. Ragi Regions

Important regions include:

  • Karnataka.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Uttarakhand and other hill regions in smaller areas.
56. Ragi in Tamil Nadu
  • Ragi is cultivated particularly in dry and upland districts.
  • Dharmapuri and Krishnagiri regions are important traditional areas.
57. Small Millets

Examples include:

  • Foxtail millet.
  • Little millet.
  • Kodo millet.
  • Barnyard millet.
  • Proso millet.
58. Millets and Climate Resilience
  • Millets can tolerate:
  • Drought.
  • High temperatures.
  • Short growing periods.
  • They are important for dryland agriculture.
59. Pulses — Importance
  • Pulses are major sources of plant protein.
  • They are important in vegetarian diets.
  • Many pulse crops improve soil fertility through nitrogen fixation.
60. Major Pulses

Important pulse crops include:

  • Gram.
  • Tur/Arhar.
  • Urad.
  • Moong.
  • Masur.
  • Peas.
61. Gram
  • Gram is chickpea.
  • It is mainly a Rabi pulse crop.
  • It prefers relatively cool and dry conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Gram → Chickpea → Rabi

62. Gram Soil
  • Well-drained loamy and black soils are suitable.
  • Excess water is harmful.
63. Tur / Arhar
  • Tur is also called pigeon pea.
  • It is mainly a Kharif pulse crop.
  • It tolerates relatively dry conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tur/Arhar → Pigeon Pea

64. Urad
  • Urad is black gram.
  • It is grown in several seasons depending on region.
  • It is an important pulse in southern India.
65. Moong
  • Moong is green gram.
  • It is a short-duration pulse.
  • It can fit well into multiple-cropping systems.
66. Pulses and Nitrogen Fixation
  • Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen.
  • Pulses therefore improve soil fertility.
67. Pulses in Tamil Nadu

Important pulses include:

  • Black gram.
  • Green gram.
  • Red gram.
  • Bengal gram in suitable dry regions.
68. Oilseeds — Overview

Important oilseeds include:

  • Groundnut.
  • Mustard.
  • Soybean.
  • Sesame.
  • Sunflower.
  • Castor.
69. Groundnut
  • Groundnut is a major oilseed crop.
  • It is mainly a Kharif crop in many areas.
  • It thrives in warm conditions and well-drained soil.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Groundnut → Important Oilseed

70. Groundnut Soil

Groundnut prefers:

  • Sandy loam.
  • Red soil.
  • Well-drained soils.

Waterlogging is harmful.

71. Groundnut Regions

Important regions include:

  • Gujarat.
  • Rajasthan.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Karnataka.
  • Maharashtra.
72. Groundnut in Tamil Nadu
  • Groundnut is widely grown in red-soil and dryland areas.
  • It is an important crop in northern and interior Tamil Nadu.
73. Mustard
  • Mustard is an important Rabi oilseed.
  • It prefers cool, dry conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mustard → Rabi Oilseed

74. Mustard Regions

Important mustard-growing regions include:

  • Rajasthan.
  • Uttar Pradesh.
  • Haryana.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
75. Soybean
  • Soybean is an important oilseed and protein crop.
  • It is mainly grown as a Kharif crop.
76. Soybean Region
  • Central India, especially Madhya Pradesh and adjoining areas, has extensive soybean cultivation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Central India → Soybean

77. Sesame
  • Sesame is also called til.
  • It is an important traditional oilseed crop.
  • It tolerates relatively dry conditions.
78. Sunflower
  • Sunflower is cultivated for edible oil.
  • It can be grown under varied climatic conditions with proper management.
79. Castor
  • Castor is an industrial oilseed crop.
  • Its oil has industrial and pharmaceutical uses.
80. Sugarcane — Basic Importance
  • Sugarcane is a major commercial crop.
  • It provides raw material for:
  • Sugar.
  • Jaggery.
  • Ethanol.
  • Bagasse.
  • Molasses.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sugarcane → Sugar + Ethanol + Bagasse

81. Sugarcane Climate

Sugarcane requires:

  • Warm climate.
  • Long frost-free growing season.
  • Adequate moisture.
  • Bright sunshine during ripening.
82. Sugarcane Water Requirement
  • Sugarcane has a relatively high water requirement.
  • Irrigation is essential in many growing regions.
83. Sugarcane Soil

It grows well in:

  • Deep fertile loams.
  • Alluvial soils.
  • Black soils under suitable conditions.
84. Major Sugarcane Regions

Important regions include:

  • Uttar Pradesh.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Karnataka.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Bihar.
  • Punjab.
  • Haryana.
85. Sugarcane in North vs South India

North India:

  • Cooler winter.
  • Shorter growing season.
  • Lower sucrose recovery in some conditions.

Peninsular India:

  • Longer warm growing season.
  • Higher sugar recovery can occur.
  • Irrigation is important.
86. Sugar Mills and Sugarcane
  • Sugarcane is bulky and loses sucrose after harvesting.
  • Mills are therefore located close to growing areas.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sugar Mill → Near Sugarcane Fields

87. Bagasse
  • Bagasse is fibrous residue remaining after sugarcane crushing.
  • It is used for:
  • Cogeneration.
  • Paper.
  • Board products.
88. Molasses
  • Molasses is a by-product of sugar manufacture.
  • It is used in:
  • Ethanol.
  • Alcohol.
  • Chemical industries.
89. Sugarcane in Tamil Nadu

Important growing areas include parts of:

  • Erode.
  • Cuddalore.
  • Villupuram.
  • Kallakurichi.
  • Tiruchirappalli.
  • Thanjavur and other irrigated regions.
90. Cotton — Basic Importance
  • Cotton is India's major natural fibre crop.
  • It is the raw material for the cotton textile industry.
  • Cotton is mainly a Kharif crop.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cotton → Kharif Fibre Crop

91. Cotton Climate

Cotton requires:

  • High temperature.
  • Moderate rainfall.
  • Bright sunshine.
  • Frost-free growing season.
92. Cotton Soil
  • Black soil is especially suitable because of its moisture-holding capacity.
  • Cotton is therefore strongly associated with the Deccan black-soil region.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cotton → Black Soil

93. Major Cotton Regions

Important cotton-growing regions include:

  • Gujarat.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Telangana.
  • Rajasthan.
  • Karnataka.
  • Madhya Pradesh.
  • Punjab.
  • Haryana.
  • Tamil Nadu.
94. Cotton and Black Soil Plateau

Important cotton regions occur in:

  • Maharashtra.
  • Gujarat.
  • Deccan Plateau states.
95. Cotton in Irrigated Northwest
  • Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan grow cotton under irrigation.
  • These regions are outside the core black-soil zone.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Cotton Can Grow Outside Black Soil with Suitable Conditions

96. Cotton in Tamil Nadu

Important cotton-growing areas occur in western and southern dry regions.

Black-soil belts favour cultivation.

97. Cotton and Textile Industry

Cotton textile industries historically developed near:

  • Cotton-growing regions.
  • Ports.
  • Markets.
  • Labour centres.
98. Jute — Basic Importance
  • Jute is a natural bast fibre.
  • It is known as the Golden Fibre.
  • It is mainly a Kharif crop.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jute → Golden Fibre

99. Jute Climate

Jute requires:

  • Warm temperature.
  • High humidity.
  • Heavy rainfall.
  • Plenty of water during processing.
100. Jute Soil
  • Fertile new alluvial soil is highly suitable.
  • Floodplains and deltaic regions favour jute.
101. Major Jute Region
  • West Bengal is the traditional core region of jute cultivation and industry.
  • The Ganga-Brahmaputra deltaic environment is highly favourable.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Jute → West Bengal

102. Jute Retting
  • Retting is the process by which jute stems are soaked in water to separate fibres from the woody stem.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jute Processing → Retting

103. Jute Uses

Jute is used for:

  • Sacks.
  • Bags.
  • Ropes.
  • Mats.
  • Packaging materials.
  • Geotextiles.
104. Mesta
  • Mesta is another bast-fibre crop.
  • It is used as a substitute or supplement to jute in some regions.
105. Tea — Basic Importance
  • Tea is a plantation beverage crop.
  • It requires:
  • Warm humid climate.
  • High rainfall.
  • Well-drained acidic soil.
  • Tea bushes are commonly grown on hill slopes.
106. Tea Soil
  • Tea prefers acidic, well-drained soil rich in organic matter.
  • Waterlogging is harmful.
107. Tea and Slopes
  • Hill slopes provide good drainage.
  • Terracing and contour planting help control erosion.
108. Major Tea Regions

Important regions include:

  • Assam.
  • Darjeeling.
  • Dooars.
  • Nilgiris.
  • Other hill regions of southern India.
109. Assam Tea
  • Assam's Brahmaputra Valley provides:
  • High rainfall.
  • Warm temperatures.
  • Humidity.
  • These conditions favour tea.
110. Darjeeling Tea
  • Darjeeling lies in the Himalayan foothills of West Bengal.
  • High elevation and cool humid conditions influence tea quality.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Darjeeling → Tea → West Bengal Hills

111. Nilgiri Tea
  • Nilgiris are Tamil Nadu's principal tea-growing region.
  • Cool highland climate and rainfall favour tea.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Tea → Nilgiris

112. Tea Labour Intensity
  • Tea requires substantial labour for:
  • Plucking.
  • Pruning.
  • Processing.
113. Coffee — Basic Importance
  • Coffee is a plantation beverage crop.
  • India grows coffee mainly in the southern hill regions.
114. Coffee Climate

Coffee prefers:

  • Warm conditions.
  • Moderate to high rainfall.
  • Well-drained soil.
  • Shade.
115. Shade-Grown Coffee
  • Indian coffee is commonly grown under shade trees.
  • Shade moderates temperature and supports biodiversity.
116. Main Coffee Types

Important commercial species include:

  • Arabica.
  • Robusta.
📌 Must-Memorise

Coffee → Arabica + Robusta

117. Major Coffee Regions

Important regions include:

  • Karnataka.
  • Kerala.
  • Tamil Nadu.
118. Karnataka Coffee
  • Karnataka's Western Ghats are India's traditional core coffee region.
  • Kodagu, Chikkamagaluru and Hassan are especially important.
119. Coffee in Tamil Nadu

Important hill regions include:

  • Nilgiris.
  • Shevaroy Hills.
  • Palani Hills.
  • Anaimalai and other suitable uplands.
120. Yercaud Coffee
  • Yercaud in the Shevaroy Hills is known for coffee and horticultural crops.
🔗 Tamil Nadu Key Link

Yercaud → Coffee → Shevaroy Hills

171. Crop Diversification
  • Crop diversification means replacing or supplementing dominant crops with a wider range of crops.
  • It can:
  • Reduce risk.
  • Improve income.
  • Save water.
  • Improve soil health.
172. Water-Saving Crop Diversification

  • Millets.
  • Pulses.
  • Oilseeds.

can reduce water demand where agro-climatically suitable.

173. Multiple Cropping
  • More than one crop is grown on the same land in a year.
  • This raises cropping intensity.
174. Sequential Cropping
  • Sequential cropping means growing crops one after another on the same field.
  • Rice-wheat is a common example.
175. Intercropping
  • Two or more crops are grown simultaneously in a planned row arrangement.
  • Examples may include cereal-pulse combinations.
176. Mixed Cropping
  • Two or more crops are grown together without a fixed row arrangement.
  • It reduces risk of total crop failure.
177. Relay Cropping
  • Relay cropping means sowing the next crop before the previous crop is harvested.
  • It reduces the time gap between crops.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

Relay Cropping → Next Crop Sown Before Previous Harvest

178. Crop Rotation
  • Crop rotation is planned succession of crops on the same land.
  • Cereal-legume rotation can improve soil fertility.
179. Fallowing
  • Leaving land uncultivated temporarily can conserve soil moisture and allow nutrient recovery.
  • Fallow periods are important in dry farming.
180. Cropping Intensity

Cropping intensity:

Gross Cropped Area ÷ Net Sown Area × 100

Higher intensity indicates more frequent use of cultivated land.

  • What is cropping pattern? → Distribution and sequence of different crops grown in a region.

  • What is molasses? → By-product of sugar processing used for alcohol and ethanol.
